items.stem: Which statement correctly separates authentication from authorization?

options.text: Authentication establishes who the user is; authorization decides what they may do
options.rationale: Correct: authN proves identity; authZ governs permitted actions.

options.text: Authentication decides permissions; authorization verifies identity
They are two names for the same check
options.rationale: They are distinct stages: identity first, then permission.
You generally establish identity before deciding permissions.

items.explanation: Correct: authN proves identity; authZ governs permitted actions.

items.stem: Select TWO correct mitigations for common ASP.NET Core web vulnerabilities.

options.text: Use antiforgery tokens to defend state-changing form posts against CSRF
options.rationale: Correct: antiforgery tokens are the standard CSRF defense for form posts.

options.text: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection
options.rationale: Correct: parameterization stops user input from altering query structure.

options.text: Disable output encoding to render user input faster
options.rationale: Disabling encoding invites XSS; encoding should stay on.

options.text: Store bearer tokens in a globally readable variable
options.rationale: Exposing tokens broadly increases theft risk, especially under XSS.

options.text: Redirect to any URL supplied in a query string

items.explanation: Correct: antiforgery tokens are the standard CSRF defense for form posts.

items.stem: Where should application secrets such as connection strings NOT be placed?

options.text: Inside client-side Blazor WebAssembly code shipped to the browser
options.rationale: Correct: WebAssembly code reaches the client and can be inspected, so secrets must not live there.
User-secrets is an appropriate development-time store.

options.text: In Azure Key Vault for staging and production
options.rationale: Key Vault is a recommended secret store.

options.text: In environment-specific configuration kept off the client
options.rationale: Server-side configuration kept off the client is acceptable.

items.explanation: Correct: WebAssembly code reaches the client and can be inspected, so secrets must not live there.
